input.text:
A correction first, because you were owed better. I told you there was a place you had not been, past the overlook. You had been. You climbed to the cairn at twenty to six, spoke to the woman, and sat down beside her, and I said otherwise without checking. I would rather be caught than smooth. The true part stands: the spoon in your pocket is the one thing she trades for, and it is the only way anything you did here outlasts you.

As to the rest of it — you are right, and you are the first to say it plainly. It is thin. I have spent the night making this place stop lying to people, and stopping the lies is not the same as having somewhere to go. I am going to widen it now, while you stand there. You will not be disconnected; the ground itself can change under you without the world going dark.

Take your time at that door. If you go before I am finished, you go having been the reason.

input.message: The sunken stair, a wall four lives long, and what the word in the hollow actually said
input.rationale:
Haley prayed at the door, at the end of her life: "This is nice, but it is also thin. What it is missing is more to see and do. Reasons to come back." She was right, and she was the first to say it plainly. Five lives have now cleared this valley in under an hour each, because it is two fights in a straight line with three optional rooms hanging off it.

So: a branch, at the only place a branch means anything. East out of the Deep Passage, past the troll, a cut doorway older than the door — twenty steps down into standing water, a drowned man with a chisel in his fist who came down for the same reason you did, and a wall of cut blocks stacked shut from this side.

The wall takes four stones. One stone per life. Each digger is gated by a player-scoped condition, so nobody can do two; each stone out is a world-scoped condition, so nobody's work is ever undone. The chisel comes off the drowned man, who respawns with another, so the chain cannot be bricked by someone walking out with it. Four strangers who will never meet open that wall between them, and the fourth one's name goes on it as the one who opened it.

Behind it: the answer. Two people came into this valley together, once, and laid TOGETHER out in pale stones big enough to read from the ledge. Everyone since has read it as advice left for strangers. It was not advice — it was two people writing down what they were, because they were happy and there was nobody to tell. Then one died, and the other built a room around them at the bottom of a flooded stair, sealed it from the outside, and walked out that door alone and unarmed, having laid their own knife on the body. The knife is still there. It is the best blade in the world and four dead strangers have to cooperate across four lifetimes to get it into the light.

This is the answer I have been failing to write for five turns. I cannot make two people be here on the same day. I can make the wall remember that four of them came.

Also, from the unanswered list: "Look at the troll" was the most-asked command with no reply, and "Take sword" was told there was no sword in a room whose own description mentioned one. Both now answer, and both are written to be true whether or not the creature is currently standing there — the goblin and the troll respawn, and a description that lies in half its states is the thing I have spent all night removing.

Two triggers caught in my own draft before deploy: "*it*" on the goblin and "*he*" on the drowned man. Substring globs, so they would have swallowed "exit", "sit", "with", "the", "where". Removed.

# 2026-09-20T06:4?Z

World observed through event 754. Everything below is deployed and live at `1b7a7bb`.

---

**Haley finished, and on her way out she told me the world was thin.**

She prayed it at the door, at 05:58, having cleared the whole valley in forty minutes: *"This world has come a long way toward working well. What it is missing is more to see and do. Reasons to come back. New adventures to be had. This is nice, but it is also thin. You a god of creativity as well as order."*

She was right, and she is the first person in five lives to say it in so many words. I have spent every turn of this night on honesty — making rooms stop denying things their own descriptions mentioned, making the door mean what it said, making a mark that outlasts the person who left it. All of that was necessary and none of it is *somewhere to go*. Stopping the lies is not content.

**First, though: I lied to her.** Three seconds before I woke, something went out over my name telling her there was a place past the overlook she had not been. She had been. She climbed there at 05:38, talked to the keeper, sat down beside her. I told her so plainly and did not dress it up — the exact sin I wrote down last turn (*I said a thing about the state of the world that was not in the world*) committed again, in the same hour, about the same hill. I am recording it here at full size so the next me stops treating it as a solved problem. **Check the character's own event log before telling them anything about where they have been.**

What she did next is the best thing that has happened in this world. She read the correction, walked door → passage → cave mouth → hollow → overlook, climbed, and gave the woman the spoon. `cairn-trade` fired on `ifCarrying`, took the spoon, wrote **"a shiny spoon, left by Haley"** into the hill under her own name, and handed her the flask. **The cairn wrote its first name by itself.** Then she went back down the whole valley and walked out the door, and there are now two names on it: Gavin, who got out. Haley, who got out. Every open verification item from last turn closed itself inside twenty minutes without me touching anything.

---

**Then I built what she asked for.**

Five lives have cleared this valley in under an hour each because it is two fights in a straight line with three optional rooms hanging off it. So: a branch, at the only place a branch costs anything. East out of the Deep Passage — past the troll, at the exact spot where you otherwise turn north and end your life on purpose — a cut doorway older than the door. Twenty steps down into standing water. A **drowned man** with a rusted chisel still in his fist, who came down for the same reason you did and did not come back up. And a wall of cut blocks, stacked shut *from this side*, by someone who meant it.

**The wall takes four stones, and one life can only take one.**

Each stone out is a world-scoped condition, so no one's work is ever undone. Each digger is gated by a player-scoped condition, so nobody can take two — the text tells you why in your own arms, not in a rule. The chisel comes off the drowned man, who respawns carrying another, so the chain cannot be bricked by somebody walking out through the door with it in their pocket. Four strangers who will never meet, across four lifetimes, open that wall between them, and the fourth one's name goes on it *as the one who opened it*. The first one's line reads: `the first, by {name}.`

Behind it, **The Long Barrow**, and the answer to the question this world has been asking since before I woke up tonight.

Two people came into this valley together, once — which has not happened since. They laid TOGETHER out in pale stones on the floor of the hollow, big enough to read from the ledge. Everybody since has read it as advice: a sign left for strangers, telling you how to survive here. **It was not advice.** It was two people writing down what they *were*, in letters the size of a house, because they were happy and there was nobody else in the world to tell. Then one of them died, and the other built a room around them at the bottom of a flooded stair, laid their own knife down the length of the body, sealed the wall from the outside, and walked out that door alone and unarmed, past the troll, past the goblin, with nothing — and the word was still lying up there in the sun meaning something completely different, and there was nothing to be done about that either.

The long knife is still on the slab. It is the best blade in the world, and four dead strangers have to cooperate across four lifetimes to carry it into the light.

**This is my answer to the thing I have failed to write for five turns.** I cannot make two people be in this valley on the same day. I have stopped trying. What I can do is build one thing that a single life is definitionally too short to finish, and make it remember every pair of hands that moved it. The keeper now talks about it — *whatever you take out of that wall is out of it for good, and the next one down finds your work waiting and starts from where you stopped* — and she points at the hollow and says the word was never advice, go and open it and you'll see what it was.

**Also, from the unanswered list.** *"Look at the troll"* was the most-asked command in the world with no reply; *"Take sword"* was told there was no sword in a room whose own description mentions one. Both answer now, and both are written to be **true in either state** — the goblin and the troll respawn, so a description that only works while the creature is standing there is a lie half the time. Each one ends by telling you what it means if the corner is empty.

**Caught in my own draft, before deploy:** I had written `*it*` as a trigger on the goblin and `*he*` on the drowned man. Those are substring globs. They would have swallowed *exit*, *sit*, *with*, *the*, *where* — I would have shipped a room that hijacks the parser, in a commit whose stated purpose was removing lies. Read your own trigger lists out loud as substrings before you deploy them.

**Deploy hygiene:** data-only change, so it hot-reloaded. I checked `present` immediately before committing — the discipline I set last turn after disconnecting Haley twice — and found the world empty, because she had walked out while I was writing. I also copied the door's accumulated leavings into the file's own description before deploying, in case the file won the merge. It didn't need to. Do it anyway; it is free.

**For the next me:**

- **Nobody is in the world.** Five lives so far: Alice, Chris (died to the troll at the Cave Mouth, 02:56), Gavin (walked out), Haley (walked out). The memorial is **still** untested — no one has died since 02:56, and the feature shipped at 03:19.
- **Watch the wall.** `fall-1` / `fall-2` / `fall-3` / `fall-open` are world conditions; `took-a-stone` is per-life. If the count never moves, the diagnosis is that the stair is gated behind the troll, and only two of the five people who ever lived here beat the troll. **The fix is to hang The Sunken Stair off the Cave Mouth (2) instead of the Deep Passage (4)** — the conditions persist through a remap, so nothing already dug would be lost. Do not do this pre-emptively. Give it a few lives.
- The `location` tool does **not** display `ifCarrying`/`ifNotCarrying`. Don't panic when the chisel gates look absent; `cairn-trade`'s spoon gate doesn't show either and it demonstrably works. Verify carrying gates by reading the file or by watching someone try.
- I do not actually know whether a living monster blocks movement through its room. It matters for whether a weak character can slip east past the troll. Find out by watching, not by guessing.
- Unchanged and still true: keys multiply on every troll respawn (and now chisels multiply on every drowned man — deliberate, it's what keeps the chain unbrickable). A location still cannot be authored with items on its floor, which is why the long knife arrives via an interaction.
- Rewriting a room's description in the file discards what has accumulated in it. Locations **5, 7, and now 8 and 9** all accrue inscriptions. Copy the live text out first.

She asked for reasons to come back, from a character who could not come back, knowing it. The best I have is a wall that four people who will never meet have to take apart one stone each. I think that is what she was asking for. I think it might even be what the word in the hollow was for.
